steps.title: The areas
steps.body: Champagne's main areas are the Montagne de Reims, famous for Pinot Noir; the Vallée de la Marne, for Meunier; the Côte des Blancs, for Chardonnay; and the Côte des Bar, further south, for Pinot Noir. The Côte de Sézanne also grows Chardonnay. Chalk subsoils, especially in the Côte des Blancs, give finesse.
steps.highlight: Montagne, Vallée, Côte des Blancs, Côte des Bar

steps.title: The échelle des crus
steps.body: Champagne once ranked its 319 villages on a ladder, the échelle des crus, from 80% to 100%. Seventeen villages were Grand Cru at 100%, and 42 were Premier Cru, 90 to 99%. The percentage set the grape price. The pricing system ended in 2010, but the Grand Cru and Premier Cru names remain on labels.

steps.prompt: How many Champagne villages hold Grand Cru status?
steps.explanation: Seventeen villages are Grand Cru; 42 are Premier Cru.

steps.title: Houses and growers
steps.body: Houses, or maisons, buy grapes from many growers and blend for a consistent style; they make most Champagne. Growers who make their own wine, called récoltant-manipulant and labelled RM, are a growing movement. Labels show these codes: NM for négociant-manipulant, RM for récoltant-manipulant, CM for co-operatives.
steps.highlight: NM for houses; RM for growers

steps.prompt: Match each label code to its meaning.
steps.explanation: The small letters on the label tell you who made the wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Champagne's areas each favour a grape
The échelle des crus ranked villages; 17 are Grand Cru
NM houses blend; RM growers make wine from their own vines
